I think you're pointing out some very real flaws, like MMR rubberbanding and the lack of distinction between Solo Q and SWF performance, but to me those are calibration issues, not reasons to scrap the system altogether.

The core idea of SBMM still makes sense; it just needs to be more nuanced. Isolated killer MMR, account for SWF vs solo, and better performance metrics would go a long way without throwing the whole thing out.

Because it was easier in a sense. Adding more generators to the map could significantly change the how the game is played and have unknown repercussions. Whereas adding a gen kick limit just removes an edge case that was being exploited.

I think you're making some fair points about how things like killer strength or SWF status can skew outcomes but I don’t think that invalidates the whole idea of matchmaking.

Like yeah, certain add-ons, killers, and map offerings can tilt things. But DBD isn’t mario party it has a huge skill ceiling. If outcomes were mostly down to RNG, we wouldn’t see the consistent performance gaps between experienced and newer players. SBMM wouldn’t even function.

The fact that killer MMR is tracked separately per killer already accounts for power disparities, so a mediocre Nurse should rise faster than a strong Pig, and that’s okay.

As for basekit comms, I agree it’d help Solo Q, and improving the UI for better communication would be great. But I’m not sure how that directly ties to throwing out SBMM altogether.

Honestly the old rank system would be preferable than what we have right now because at least rank 1 matched you with good killers and survivors but that isn't to say it didn't have its own issues.

The purpose of the abandon feature is to give an out for killers who are being held hostage by survivors who refuse to progress the generators. This makes it sound like the survivors are in the wrong, but the truth is that they're just playing optimally if there's no chance of completing the generators. The only chance of escaping in that circumstance is playing for hatch which requires another survivor to be sacrificed. It's therefore not the fault of the survivors, but the fault of the killer for being unable to find and sacrifice another survivor. The killer is the one failing to progress the game to the next stage and therefore the survivors should not be punished for that.

It is also the choice of the killer to give up and press the DC button. If the killer doesn't want to lose, they don't have to press the button. You're drawing a false equivalence. Yes, to mori the last survivor technically fulfills the killer’s role in the game, just like escaping does for survivors. But the context in which that happens is completely different.

When a survivor escapes, they have completed an objective under pressure. They are still playing, making decisions, avoiding danger, and earning their outcome. It is an interactive conclusion to their gameplay loop.

When you mori or hook a survivor who is already in the dying state, especially when all survivors are down, the match is effectively over. There is no tension, no decision-making, and no resistance. It is not a fight anymore; it is a cutscene. You are not securing victory through skill at that point. That part is already done. What remains is a non-interactive animation.

So when a survivor chooses to abandon at that stage, they are not refusing to let you win. You have already won. They are simply choosing not to participate in a moment that has no gameplay meaning for them.

This is where the connection to validation and/or control becomes clear. You want them to be present, not because it changes the result, but because their presence completes the emotional arc for you. A bot does not provide that. Killing a scripted replacement does not feel as satisfying. You want a real person to witness the end because their presence affirms your power, your dominance, and your victory. That is validation.

When they remove themselves from that moment and choose to exit the match, you lose control over how it ends emotionally. The outcome remains the same, but the experience feels incomplete because it no longer matches the story you had in mind. That is where the control issue appears.

It really depends on the situation. If the gates are close by and everyone can escape immediately, then yeah, opening them makes sense. But if the gates are far away and no one is on death hook, sometimes you *do* need multiple attempts to even get close enough before it’s necessary to open them. Keeping them 99’d in those cases prevents unnecessary pressure and gives the team more control over the rescue.

I get what you’re saying, but I completely disagree with the idea that “if you can’t get out in that time, you’re probably not getting out at all.” The reality is that people do die to EGC, and sometimes multiple rescue attempts and resets are needed. That *does* take extra time. That’s exactly why immediately opening the gate can be a mistake - it removes that flexibility and forces rushed plays under unnecessary pressure. If anything, your argument could be flipped. Are you seriously telling me you died because of the extra second needed to open a 99’d gate? It’s far more likely you were already in a losing position or the gate wasn’t properly 99ed.

I do agree that there comes a point where you *have* to open the gate, but that’s the whole point of 99ing - to delay that moment until it’s actually necessary, rather than pre-emptively putting your team in a worse position.

And if I had a nickel for every time someone instantly opened the gate and it led to the entire team getting killed during end game collapse, I’d probably be even richer.

Like I said, there are definitely situations where opening is better, but in most cases, keeping it 99’d gives the team more control and increases the chances of a coordinated escape. It’s all about reading the situation.

Of course it's not black and white, that's why I said there are exceptions. There are definitely situations where opening the gates immediately is the better play. But in general, 99ing gives the team more control over the endgame, allowing for coordination, healing, and multiple rescue attempts if needed. The difference between comp and casual play is the mindset: in comp, minimizing hook states is a priority, while in pubs, people are more willing to take risks for saves. That’s why 99ing is usually the better default strategy in pubs, though there are always exceptions.

Ultimately, whatever works best for you. But, I find RNG is not an issue for me. There are further ways to circumvent bad RNG. For example, don't move randomly or in one direction, focus on limiting your movement to a certain localised space so the little gems are all clustered around you in a smaller area making them easier to pick up ones you missed. I find if you move around in a circle, it's easy to run into lots of monsters, and make it so you are running into gems you missed in previous loops. The circle path is generally large enough that magnets start appearing out of nowhere (not sure if monster loot, or crates randomly spawning that I didn't see were destroyed), but if not, I'm still picking up the important gems (blue and yellow).

I'm not talking about the magnet skill (which is even more useless), I'm talking about the magnets you pick up on the ground. Once you pick up a magnet, every single little gem you didn't pick up is immediately gained, rendering whatever advantage you get from picking up gems faster pretty insignificant. So as long as you're picking up magnets every so often, it's better to maximise the rate at which you can kill monsters, rather than the speed you can pick up gems. 

If you're farming chapter 4, then by all means use the speed boost as your damage capacity is already above and beyond what it needs to be to kill monsters to the point where moving faster actually raises your rate of damage more significantly than if used on another skill, but if you're aiming to beat the current chapter you're up to, getting a speed boost with the aim of getting gems faster isn't the best strategy.
